definition: Ornament means an object or feature added to something to make it more attractive.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word ornament. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know ornament should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The old theater's ceiling is crowded with plaster ornaments — rosettes, vines, and gilded leaves added purely to delight the eye.
An accent is just a small decorative touch; an ornament is a full decorative object in its own right.
A showpiece goes beyond an ornament — it's the star attraction, meant to impress everyone who enters the room.

Decoration is the broadest word for anything added to make a thing prettier — from birthday streamers to gold leaf — and it can name the whole prettifying scheme. An ornament is one distinct decorative object, added purely to please the eye. Decorations may blanket a room; each carved rosette is an ornament.

An adornment is a decorative touch that beautifies something, and the word leans toward what is worn or draped — jewels, garlands, embroidery. An ornament is a free-standing decorative object in its own right, often part of a building or display. A necklace is an adornment; the carved rosette above a door is an ornament.

A trinket is a small, showy object of little practical value — the kind of thing collected on a shelf or won at a fair. An ornament can be finely made and genuinely treasured; what defines it is being added purely for beauty. A trinket is cheap by definition; an ornament need not be.

Ornament means an object or feature added to something to make it more attractive.
The blacksmith welded a curling iron leaf onto the garden gate — not for strength, just as an ornament.
The iron leaf does no structural work at all; its only job is to make the gate more beautiful.
Anything added purely for looks — never for function — is an ornament.
An ornament is added and non-functional — take it away and the object still works, it just looks plainer.
The most familiar everyday use is holiday tree ornaments, but architecture, jewelry, and writing can all carry ornament too.
The adjective is 'ornamental' ('a purely ornamental balcony').

When the city rebuilt the Fourth Street bridge, the plans were all girders and load limits — except for one odd line item: four cast-iron pelicans, one for each corner post.
The pelicans held nothing up.
They carried no wire, shaded no walkway, and cost eleven thousand dollars the auditors tried twice to cut.
The chief engineer defended them in a single sentence: a bridge people love is a bridge people maintain.
Each pelican is an ornament in the strict sense — an object with no job except to please the eye of whoever crosses.
Sixty years on, the girders have been replaced twice, but when one pelican cracked in a storm, the city recast it within a month, from the original mold.
